title: Philip K. Dick and the Umbrella of Light
author: Angus Taylor
card_summary: An early critical monograph on Philip K. Dick by Angus Taylor, originally published in 1975 by T-K Graphics, Baltimore, with illustrations by Cora Lee Healy. Parts of the work appeared earlier in the British journal Foundation (No. 4, July 1973) under the title 'Can God Fly? Can He Hold Out His Arms and Fly?' The work is structured in three parts examining monsters from outer and inner space, the willing extension of disbelief, and the concept of the 'umbrella of light.' This edition is a 2025 reformatted reissue with minor corrections. A significant early work of PKD literary criticism.
page_summary:
Philip K. Dick and the Umbrella of Light is a critical monograph by Angus Taylor, published by T-K Graphics of Baltimore in 1975, with illustrations by C. Lee Healy. Parts of the work appeared earlier in the British journal Foundation, No. 4, July 1973, in an article titled "Can God Fly? Can He Hold Out His Arms and Fly?"

This is one of the earliest book-length critical studies devoted to Dick's work, published during Dick's lifetime. Taylor's study examines Dick's fiction through the lens of his philosophical and theological concerns, with the title referencing the imagery of light and transcendence that pervades Dick's later work. The original Foundation article from 1973 places Taylor's criticism alongside other early academic engagements with Dick in British science fiction criticism.

T-K Graphics was a small press that published several science fiction critical works during the 1970s. Taylor's monograph represents a pioneering effort to treat Dick's work as worthy of sustained critical analysis at a time when science fiction was still struggling for academic respectability. The work is now a collector's item and an important document in the history of Dick criticism.

## Introduction 

“So you maintain,” Doug Appleford said briskly, “that if a person is killed by a meteor it’s because he hated his grandmother. Some theory.” ( _Counter-Clock World_ , ch. 16) 

t is only in the last few years that much serious attempt has been made to understand the nature of science fiction as a genre and its I place within the context of literature as a whole. The editors and writers of the pulp magazines too often saw science fiction in simplistic terms of prediction or extrapolation, even while their own stories belied their claims. A slightly more sophisticated view holds that the function of science fiction is the mapping out of the realistic possibilities of the future; along this line Robert A. Heinlein can maintain that sciencefiction writers are the futurologists of fiction.[1] But what these critics have tended to ignore is the poetic quality of the literature. Science fiction is not first and foremost science; it is first and foremost fiction. It has developed within a historical context that has given to it its unique qualities, but it shares something with all fiction, and with all art: it attempts to transcend its own materials and evoke another reality. Camus has described how the artist works through selection, by isolating the unique in the context of the universal. The artist plucks an instant from passing time and gives it a permanence, but a permanence shaped by the artist’s own vision. C. S. Lewis has likened the series of events that occurs within a story to a net designed to catch an elusive something else. “The real theme may be, and perhaps usually is, something that has no sequence in it, something other than a process and much more like a state or quality.”[2] 

The proper study of science fiction, then, removes it from the technocratic ghetto and confronts the issue of its relation to so-called literature. Recent attempts at defining the genre have tended to crystallize around two perspectives: the sociological, and what may be called the “formal”.
